title: Regression Language Models for Code
claim: One unified encoder-decoder model reads heterogeneous code and graph inputs as text and predicts diverse numeric metrics.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right: inputs, central model block, output panels with plot
description: Left-to-right diagram with three zones. On the left, two groups of inputs sit under the headings 'Code Regression (Memory, Latency)' and 'Graph Regression (Accuracy, Latency)'. The code group is a grid of navy-headed code snippet cards for C++, Triton, Haskell and Python, with ellipses between them. The graph group has an ONNX Graph text snippet and a node-link graph plot. Its nodes are colored as input, weights, activations and output. In the center, a large gray box labeled 'Regression Language Model' holds two inner boxes, 'Encoder (T5Gemma)' and 'Decoder'. A large arrow points right from it. On the right, three stacked cards cover CPU code memory estimation, Triton kernel latency estimation and multi-objective regression. Each card has a hardware icon. The last card shows a Pixel3 accuracy-versus-latency scatter plot with a density overlay.
caption: A Regression Language Model (RLM) is able to simultaneously read code from many different languages and compilation levels, and predict metrics such as accuracy, memory, and latency.
abstract: We study code-to-metric regression: predicting numeric outcomes of code executions, a challenging task due to the open-ended nature of programming languages. While prior methods have resorted to heavy and domain-specific feature engineering, we show that a single unified Regression Language Model (RLM) using a frozen LLM encoder can simultaneously predict directly from text, (i) the memory footprint of code across multiple high-level languages such as Python and C++, (ii) the latency of Triton GPU kernels, and (iii) the accuracy and speed of trained neural networks represented in ONNX. In particular, a relatively small 300M parameter RLM based on T5Gemma, obtains >0.9 Spearman-rank on competitive programming submissions from APPS, and a single unified model achieves >0.5 average Spearman-rank across 24 different programming languages from CodeNet. Furthermore, the RLM can obtain the highest average Kendall-Tau of 0.46 on five classic NAS design spaces previously dominated by graph neural networks, and simultaneously predict architecture latencies on numerous hardware platforms.
